blocks.x: Okay, we're interviewing today at 1722 New Orleans Street, that's right. Let's see, what's today's date, folks? 22nd. June the 22nd, 1960. And who are we interviewing? What's that mean? Lewis Bobrin. That's your full name? Lewis Isidall Bobrin.
Same as your father's name. My father's name, I think.
Your father's name was Isidall. Yeah, that's right. Don't know.

I'm going to put the microphone right here and hopefully it doesn't pick up too much of the fan noise. You all need a fan? Don't cut it out. Maybe we can cut it out. I'll take it off. Cut it out. Pick up. Yeah. Pick up that squeak in there.

Okay, I'll put my name. Dick Allen. Bill? This is Bill Russell. Ralph Collins. Okay. All right. I think that's a good introduction there. Everybody knows which voice it is on the tape when they hear it.

Do you want to start out when you were born? Just anything you have your notes there if you want to follow that would be fine. You want to, when you're ready? Yeah. I learned how to play the drums. Right?
Everything we've done since we've done. Yeah, we'd like to get your birthday next time. You all ready now?
Mm-hmm. It's on? It's on. Yeah.
Oh.

I learned drums by playing on my mother's chairs, the two forks. That was in the year of 1916. My father bought my brother, Paul, a set of drums. And Paul was playing around here with different bands. And he was called to Chicago to play with Manuel Ferrer's band at the Royal Garden in Chicago. My first set of drums was the one Paul was working with in Chicago. And he sent them to me because he bought some new ones. Well, I was on the way to start playing the first job. I played a house party, just a piano and drums. The musicians around here heard how well I was playing and hired me to play with them. They were not organized. And I would go to different dances. And Sam Morgan's band and Kid René's band were playing. And they would let me sit in and play with them. I became known. The name bands would start hiring me. Sam Morgan, Kid René, Jack Carey, Kid Punch, AJ Piron's band. I played at Tom Anderson's Night Spot in 1923 on Rampart Street near Canal in the Red Light District. The years of 1923, an organized band named Imperial Serenaders gave me my break. I played with them around here a while. And they'd taken a job at the Victory Inn, a night spot on the Jefferson Highway. Albert Snider, the trumpet man who was in charge of the band, had a day job. And he said he would not quit to play at night. So at that time, Sidney Desvane had came in from St. Louis off the Steamer Capital. And he'd taken a job playing trumpet in the band. And the band's name was changed to Sudden Syncopator. We played on the Steamer Capital and the Island Queen of Cincinnati. Red Island and Pop Foster was with the band at that time. I started playing with Poppa Celestine's band in 1937. And in the 40s, I started with Sidney Desvane's band again. In 1947, I went to New York with Danny Barker, speculating on his job. And I got the USO group. Was going to Japan. So I made the trip. Played Manila Okinawa in Japan. June 1948. I was back in the States. Started back with Sidney's band until 1950. Then I joined Poppa Celestine's band. We were playing at the Paddock Lounge. And I quit because I did not think much of the job. So I went to work at the Elmer Rock with Joy Lewis' group. And I played with them six months. The job closed. And I went to a famous dole. And played there about three months. And the contract ended. I went back with Celestine's group. And here I am.
I don't believe you gave us your birth date exactly. And just what part of the city you were born in. I didn't want that. Right at the very beginning. Okay. I was born in New Orleans.
October 24, 1902.
What part of town? Remember the street?
Oh, the street.
I was born on...
Let's see. I was... Liberty. St. Claude and... What's the street here? Columbus and St. Claude. Columbus and St. Claude.

Not far from here then. That's right. Your father lived there long. Did he live... Yeah, we lived there quite a while. Where was Paul? Born in the same place about... Had you lived there quite a while? Do you remember? I don't remember. I just can't remember. How much older is Paul than you? I forget.
Well, I'm 57. 57. I was... 362, I believe.
Could you tell us some more about your other brothers that played music?

I have another brother. Well, he's learning trumpet. William Barber. He played around with several organized groups and... But he never did keep it up. Lucien Barber and my other brother, which passed, he played with the D and... Billy?
Billy and the D.
Yeah.
Can you remember any more about him? Did he take any lessons? No, he never did take any lessons.
What did he play?
Drums. Yeah, he played drums.
He'd been a good drummer, too. Was he younger than you? Yeah, he was younger than me.
About how many years?
Well, two years different. Oh, two years. Two years different.
Well, did he play with anybody else, you say, besides... Did he? Well, I know. Did he start on your drum?

Well, I learned him some drums. Yeah, I did. Can you tell us any more about when you started? Did your brother help you, Paul? Had he been playing long before that that you can remember? Well, Paul was playing long before I started. I knew he was older, of course. Yeah, he was playing long. Playing around with different bands around the office. Did he help you any? Did he show you how to hold the sticks or anything? Well, he did. Give me ideas. Paul, give me ideas. Did your father ever teach you anything about music that isn't reading music? No.
I've taken my drum lesson from Cottrell. Lewis Cottrell.
Did you tell us more about him?

Well, all I know is he's one of the finest drummers around the city of New Orleans, I can tell you that. That's what everybody said. Played with Excelsior Brass, brass man. Yeah, it was techno. How long did you go to him? All about a few months, six, seven months until he passed.
But at the end of his life, when was that? Do you remember when he died? We'll get that information from his son, of course.
Well, I was wondering, how old were you when he died? You might know roughly.
Oh, I just can't say no one year that was then. One more year. The only one I can tell, that's his son, his son, Lewis. Yeah, he'll tell us his son. Yeah, he'll tell us his son.
Yeah, he'll tell us his son. Well, actually, you were pretty much a grown man before you took drum lessons.
Well, I was, let's see, in the 20s. I was around 18 years old, sure.
Before you took lessons from him, huh? And then, let's see, well, he made records in 24. He made that in New York.
Oh, with Pierron. Oh, yeah, they played, they made this recording of Sister Kate. They had West Vietnamese Blues. Anybody want to buy my cabbage? That's the recording they made of.
Yeah, they made quite a few out there.
Yeah, they have a lot of them.
So he must have died after he came back here.
Oh, yeah, after he came from New York, yeah.
Were you playing long before you took lessons from him?
Well, I was playing with all the organized groups, you know. Before you ever took any lessons? Yeah, before I was taking them.
What did he emphasize in teaching you? Did he emphasize the snare drum, the bass drum, or any particular...
No, I was the snare drum.
He tried to teach you that, huh?
Snare drum, yeah. Good roll, you know. Did you use a drum pad at first? Well, I used a drum pad.
Before you went to the actual drum pad.
Yeah, actual drums, yeah, drum pad.
Did you teach anything about patting your foot?
Well, yeah, you know how to beat time, you know.
How would he show you? What would he tell you?
Well, just hold my feet. And count? Yeah, I'd count a whole lot, yeah.
Would you count for every time you beat your foot down?
My foot down, yeah. I'm a tempo and everything.

Can you tell us anything about the very earliest music you heard when you were a boy? What the bands were like? Were they the brass bands that your father played in or any dance bands? What can you remember when you were just a little kid?

Well, when I knew about music, I got to follow these parades. My dad used to play with Lil Armstrong. Lil Armstrong had to come out to Waves Home then, see. And sometimes the Waves Home band would play in these big parades, you understand what I mean? And Lil's was with the band, see. And after Lil's got out of the home, then he joined my daddy and them, see. I believe it was the Arnold Brass Band, the Olympia Brass Band they had at that time, Imperial Brass Band.
Do you remember much about your father when you were young? Did he practice at home very much? Oh, yeah, my dad always practiced.
He was always practicing? Always practiced. I have my dad's home here now. The alto. I had the melaphone.
The melaphone.
I have it here on the alto.
I'd like to see that before we leave. I really want to know.
What kind it is and everything. Did he ever play anything else around the home, a cornet or barricade?

No, his instrument was first instrument, it was cornet. That's what I thought he started. His first instrument was cornet, then he had alto, brass alto, then the melaphone. That's his last instrument.
When you followed him, what band was he playing with?

Oh, the Arnold Band. I played with the Arnold Band too. Oh. Brass Band. Yeah, Man Forrest, my dad, Ernest Rappanian. Yeah. I was playing snap drum, and Ernest Rappanian was playing bass drum. How was he, Ernest Rappanian? Oh, he's fine. Fine drummers. Yes, yeah.
Could you give me an idea of what his beat would be like? Would he have a lot of double rap stuff, or would he play it?

Well, yeah, he played double raps, yeah. I just couldn't hum it to him. You couldn't hum it, huh? I couldn't hum it the way he played. Yeah, hum a little bit of it. We played boom, all that kind of stuff he played.
Sounds like it would really sing you, huh?
Oh, yeah. Yeah, we're just not, we're just, he know where to put the licks in, you know?
How big a drum did he use? Do you remember how big a drum was?

Well, yeah, the drums at that time ought to have been around 14, 26, I should have been 26 for the parade that time. I don't believe you were 28 that time. I believe 28 was too, no, I believe 28 at that time. They carried those on the street, too. 28, I believe, yeah, because the 26 was a little mired, and then they came down to 24, and he was 22, 98, and 2018 now. I believe it was around the 28 they were using at that time.
Did he use two bass drum beaters?
No, one. And the cymbal on top.
How big a cymbal did he have?

And the cymbal beater. Well, the cymbal was about, I'll say about 14 in cymbal. Yeah, just about a 14 in cymbal. You used a wire beater? Wire beater, that's correct, yeah. You hit the cymbal with the leg? Left hand, correct, yeah. The bass drum.
How would he hit that cymbal?
Well, I'll tell you how it's done. The bass drum's right hand, and that has a strap. The bass drum's front, and here it is. On the half beat, see? Bass drum's on the down beat. After. After.
In other words, it'd go, we count one, two, three, four. It'd be one with the right hand, two with the left, three with the right, four with the left.
That's correct. That's right.
But did you play two, four, or four, four in the street?
No. I'll tell you how they did it. They played two, four, as it's marching. And on the out chorus, then they played four, four, going out.
You hear that today, it's very similar.
Yeah, sometimes they do that now. They do it now.
Did you ever play bass drum in parades?
No, I never did.
Just snare drum.
Snare drum.
When you were young, who were some of the outstanding snare drummers and bass drum players, even before you started playing?
Oh, well, I can tell you, that was Henry Martin. I know you have heard of him. I've heard of him.
I've never got one.
Red Dugal.
You ever heard of him? Never, I've heard of him, but never knew much about him. You know anything about him, especially? No, he's a fine drummer. What part of town he came from?
He came from around the Red Light District. Bienvenida, Vilcona, Liberty. Benny.
Yeah.
I know his first name. I know you know Benny. Like Benny. Like Benny.
Who were these guys playing with, like Henry Martin, Red Dugal, and Black Benny?

Well, they was playing with the Armored Band, Brass Band. All three of them? Yeah, but not three drummers at one time. Different bands, different brass bands they played with. Excelsior Band, Olympia Band, Imperial Band.
Did they all play one particular drum, like snare or bass, or did they play them both?
No, they played one drum in the parade. That's all snare drum.
Well, for instance, which drum would Henry Martin play?
Snare drum. What about Benny? Benny would play bass drum.
I heard you played bass drum.
Well, yeah, that's a fact of them, but I know of them. I followed them around.
What about Red Dugal? What did he play?
Snare drum. Well, he played orchestra drums too, you know, in orchestra. Henry Martin played orchestra drums too.
What orchestras would they play with?
Well, they was playing in nightclubs in the district, see. But I was young again, I just can't remember.
We talked to your father about a year ago, of course, but a lot of things we didn't ask him. It was a little difficult, you know, he couldn't hear something.
He was sick at the time, yeah.
But do you remember, did he ever play any dance bands at all, orchestra work, or just all these brass bands? Well, I'll tell you.
I played, we played picnics on the 30th of May. That'd be a big day in your, 10th of May, the 30th of May. And we played the picnics like the Seda, like the Vardalia's picnic, like that.

and excursions like that. My dad should go to King Oliver and then they'd play excursions out of Littlewood like that. And they'd go down for us to Point Lahash to have excursions, train excursions. And he'd also play picnics at the fairground like that. Set the big band up and see, and people would dance. With the brass band? With the brass band, by the brass band. That's correct. I played too. I played with the violi-dadi's picnics at the fairground and I was taking a sick tonight playing snare drum. Not taking a sick I ate some potatoes out of a galvanized tub they had there, you know, and ingesting it. Potato salad, what you call it.
That put you out of commission for that game. Huh? That put you out of commission for the rest of the game.
Oh yeah, for a while I really was out of commission. Was your father ever playing in any small groups, do you think, like a seven or eight piece No.
No. No. No. No.
No. No. No. Who else was in that Arnold band? I wanted to get all the other guys.
Well, I'm gonna tell you. If I can remember.
Mm-hmm.
Well, they had my dad, Mario Perez, Ernest Rapana, Eddie Sherry, you heard of him. I believe Adolf Alexander.
Let's get the instruments too, I'm confused. Now, Eddie Sherry played what?
Clarinet.
E flat or B flat?

I believe he played E flat clarinet, a small clarinet. E flat I believe he played, if I'm not mistaken. But they used E flat on parades. That's what they did. And Adolf Alexander played Adolf Alexander played alto sax. I believe in. And Ernest Rapana was a snare drum player. Bass drum player. You will scratch that out. Yeah, don't worry about it.
That's all right.

All right then. Ernest Rapana was the bass drum player. Sometimes they would, I believe Alfred Williams played snare drum. The trumpet player had, you heard of Maurice Durand. I believe Maurice Durand was in the band at that time. Man for Rest and Maurice Durand. They had three trumpets I believe. I'm trying to think the other trumpet player. I believe, I Andrew Kimball. You heard of Andrew Kimball. I'm positive. And on the front line they had two tromones. They had Buddy Johnson, you heard of Buddy Johnson, Mal Jis. And I believe his brother Yank, he might have heard of his brother. He had two trombone brothers playing trombone
at that time. Do you remember George Peele on trombone? Did he ever play with Manuel in any

of those? I don't remember George Peele. I don't remember. If he did, he played in New Orleans with the brass band I remember. But I know he was in Chicago and he had parents living on the brass band. He was in San Anner Street in New Orleans before he died. And I didn't know much about George Peele. My daddy always talked about George Peele and George Bocquet and a lot of others. But I don't know George Bocquet. My daddy would tell me about him,
Brian Clarenidison. What about tuba player with the Arnold?

Well the Arnold band was Eddie Jackson I believe, I recall. Eddie Jackson. Did they have an alto horn or a baritone horn? Yeah. Alexander played, Adolph Alexander played baritone senior. That's Adolph's daddy. Tats' daddy. Living right about a block from here on the corner of me now. They don't stay there now, but they was staying there at the time. That's Tats' daddy. And he's passed. He passed too, yeah. He played baritone, he played euphonium too. I think he was an arranger. Well he used to write music and politics. Somebody told me to arrange some
for fellas. Bill Matthews I guess. And I remember another fine drummer too. They called Bill Matthews'

brother. I forget his other name. They called him Bebe Matthews. You ever heard of that? Yeah, he just died didn't he? Yeah. Happy just died. But this is the older, I believe this is one of the brothers that played Manny Paris around here when they had the orchestra. Yeah, Bebe had been dead long time ago. Long time ago, but he was a fine drummer.
What did he feature? Oh, he played orchestra drums. But I mean would he feature cymbal work
a snare? No, snare, snare weight. Yeah. Did he have a good role? Oh yeah, fine roller, fine drummer.
Did they hold their sticks in any different ways or make the rolls in any funny kind of
ways? Well a lot of, a lot of guys nowadays they don't, they hold different positions.
I might get an idea. Yeah, we can wait a minute, we'll turn it off.

Right position. That's the standard. Is it the, I've described it. The left hand, the two fingers on top. That's right. And the, uh, I've seen people hold the, uh, the right hand differently. Well I'll tell you it's a lot different. When that wiggles, does it, some people I've seen hold it mostly with these fingers and they'll say wiggle it.

You see you have, you have, you have like a, like brakes. Like you're gonna, if you don't have brakes on these fingers, something has to stop these sticks. Yeah, that's right. They'll just shake out of your hand. That's right. What you call a bumper light. So you've got, excuse me, go ahead. Everything's, uh, you roll, you don't use the whole body. It's all done from the wrist.

You don't hold, you use all your arms or anything. I notice you, you hold it about two thirds of the way, uh, up from the, from the bead. They say you don't hold it very close to the end there with your left hand. No. That's right. Do you find that's a better balance there? It is. You're saying, you're better reaction I believe.
Your sticks are fairly heavy on the, uh, well I don't, I don't use these sticks. It's practice sticks. Oh, those practice sticks. Yeah.

Those are the S sticks they call, uh, something, one S or something, something, they have a number on them. Yeah, they, yeah. They're big heavy ones for the street. Yeah, this is naturally practice sticks, that's all. Three S, it says, yeah. Yeah, it's practice. Ludwig. That's Ludwig, yeah. Three, three S. Yeah.

I notice you hold it with your right hand about the same balance as the left, just about there. Uh, and you have all four fingers and a full finger controlling it with your right hand and the thumb too, really. You don't grip it up between your thumbs and thumbs. I'll give you, you want to get an idea about a roll? Yeah. Yeah. Let me get my pad, yeah? Yeah. Yeah.

Thank you, Will. Yeah, I think the, uh, as long as you have the pad there, that'll be fine. Okay. See what it did with the sticks. Oh, yeah. I did. You think I'll pick it up? While I think of it, I don't believe you mentioned in your story that you, I did not. Oh, pardon. That you, that you do teach, um, I teach, yeah. How to desecute, gateway. Gateway, correct. You're still there, are you? Well, no, I'm not there since they, uh, they separated the branch. See, the branch had,

colored branch is not there anymore. Well, I never heard of them. See, I used to, I was teaching after a while too. Yeah. But Mr. Levine have, uh, school back here on, uh, Auburn and Retroblades. He wanted me to come out. I don't have enough students. Yeah. After a while they had the GI Bill of Rights. It was, uh, it was fine then. And then there was a lot of fellow studying. You gotta wait until the summer, school is out and the summer session is starting. Uh-huh. Kids come in, you know, and take about eight lessons, you know. After that, you don't see them anymore. Yeah. You see, you were going to demonstrate some things on the drum pad. I can't, I can't, you know. Five stroke roll, seven stroke roll, nine stroke roll. I'll, I'll, I'll demonstrate the five stroke roll, alright? Yeah. Alright. That's a five. Seven. That's a nine stroke. Sounds good. Now this, uh, here's the, uh, open roll. Close roll.
Now, uh, just a minute, uh, what's the difference there? Aside from being slower. One, one's open, one's closed.
What, what do you mean by open and closed? Alright, here's the open here. Not wide that is. Not closed. Ah. Not closed.
On the closed roll, your sticks stay close to the, uh, close to the head. That's right. Close to the head. Uh, now the difference there would be that the open roll would be a little louder.

A little louder. Be separated like, oh, oh. Now the difference, now listen at the difference. Now a little rough for you if you want. What, what that? That's a rough. That's the rough. Yeah. What, what, what does that say? Well that's, uh, that's just a grace note to beautify the note. That's all it is. Oh, I see. You're just putting something just to, uh, say beautify the note. See if you, that's nothing. That's, what is the drag? Is that similar to that? That's what, similar to the drag. That's correct. That's right.
Well, uh, what is a press roll? Press roll? Sure. That's a press roll.
I'll try that again. Do you let both the sticks bounce or just the one? No, no. One behind the other.
Alright, first stick on here, I'm playing my left hand. Then come down both. That's your lead off. That's your beat. Your lead off is on the other.
Where does it get the name press roll from, Willa? Well, I don't know. Are you sort of pressing down on it? Well, I, I, I just can't, I wouldn't say.

Does the right hand bounce more usually, I understand, on the roll. Each stick bounces twice. Does it bounce several times on the press roll? Yeah, that's right. Just keeps on pressing. Is there anything out there, strokes that you practice on, like paradiddle and all those? I don't remember how it's called, but, uh, that's just, you know. That's all. That's all. How's that in, in terms of left, right, left, left, or how is it? Yeah. Yeah.
Down, You start with the right. Right, yeah. Right. Either way you can alternate. Yeah. Start with either hand. That's right. Right.
Caught in. Anything else, Dick, that you wanted to ask? We got another minute or two there, if there is anything.
Yeah, uh, could we, uh, stop in a minute so we could describe the horn?
Going again. Let's talk about that horn for a minute.
Okay.
Silver plate in the first place. What make is it? See, just, wait now.
See how you call it?
No, I didn't call it. Frank Holden, huh? That's Holden? Yeah. Frank Holden and Company, Al Hong.
That's one of the good makes though, right? Yeah. It's in perfect shape, isn't it? Mm-hmm.
And it's a mellophone. Mellophone, that's right. Here's the bit, see? That's the bit they call it.
Can you play it?
I was, I was learning how to play this horn, but I got away from it. It's in perfect, it's in perfect condition.
My dad gave me that just before he was dead. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. He told me that he had it. He told me that he had it.

When was his last job about? Do you remember his last parade or his job? Probably made the records I think after he quit marching maybe. No. I don't remember for sure. I don't just remember. You don't remember when he played his last parade? No, I don't remember that.
It's a number two holds on my piece I see. I guess that came with a horn.
Yeah.
How do you hold it? With your hand in the bell there?

Some of them, yeah they play with the hand in the bell I'm sure they do some of them. Is that the way your father played it? I believe he used to play it. Sometime I've seen him with the hand in the bell.
He'd start to change it around to Susan's house.
Yeah.
Do you remember that bell?
No, I don't remember exactly how he held it. No. I saw him play a parade or two and then he made some records with bunks. Yeah, he made records.

I know these guys have been so long and I know who they work with, but as the years go by you forget. Like in Kid René's band, Zip, a fine clarinet player. You ever hear of Maurice French? Why don't you fellas go pick up Maurice French? You know where a lot of Maurice French was at? I was at his home about three weeks ago. I played out in a high school out there and I talked to Maurice French. He's in Laplace. He's in a Resort, they go to Laplace. I got it from Albert. You got it from Albert?
But not the exact address.
I could run up there with Punch sometime. I wonder if he ever worked with Punch. That would be fun.
He'd go up there and Morris would give you the whole lowdown on this time. That's right.
Did you play with him in the old days?
I played with Kid Rene's band. He was playing Rene's band at the time. Joe Rene's playing. I used to play sometimes. Joe couldn't play and I played sometimes.
Who else was in Rene's band?
Well that was Rene, Zeb, Morris French. The band you play was... Oh, what's the spell name again? I believe it was T-Boy. You hear about it?
I've heard of him.
You heard of him?
Yeah, I've heard the name too. No, that's... I'm thinking of a bass band.
No, T-Boy's a bass player. They got T-Boy Rene and me play trumpet too, you know. Yeah, then they got a T-Boy, I believe he was playing bands with Kid Rene too.
How did he look like?
Well, he was brown skinned, slim brown, with big eyes I believe.
Was he sharp?
No, it was about his height. Not Ralph's height? Yeah, not as tall as him. About his height, it's about his height.
Hey, Lewis, I meant to ask you, did you ever know any other name for Zeb? Zeb?

segments.title: Interview opening and setup
segments.summary: Allen and Russell introduce the date, place and interviewee and set up the microphone.

segments.title: Career summary: first drums to Celestin's band
segments.summary: Barbarin sums up how he got Paul's drums, sat in with Sam Morgan and Kid Rena, joined the Imperial Serenaders, the Steamer Capitol, Celestin, Desvigne and the 1947 USO tour.

segments.title: Birth date and birthplace
segments.summary: Born October 24, 1902 near Columbus and St. Claude; he is unsure of details about Paul's age.

segments.title: His brothers who played music
segments.summary: He describes his brothers William, Lucien and a younger drummer brother who played with Billie and De De.

segments.title: Paul's help when he started drumming
segments.summary: Paul was already playing and gave him ideas, but his father taught him nothing about music.

segments.title: Drum lessons from Louis Cottrell
segments.summary: He studied with Cottrell for six or seven months at about eighteen, after already playing in organised groups; Cottrell's later records with Piron are mentioned.

segments.title: What Cottrell taught: snare roll, pad and counting time
segments.summary: Cottrell stressed snare drum and a good roll, practice on a pad, and beating time with the foot while counting.

segments.chapter: Father and the brass band tradition
segments.title: Following his father's brass band as a boy
segments.summary: As a boy he followed parades; his father played with the Waifs' Home band and later the Onward, Olympia and Imperial brass bands, on cornet, alto and mellophone.

segments.chapter: Father and the brass band tradition
segments.title: Brass band drumming: Perez's band, drum sizes and street beat
segments.summary: Barbarin played snare in the Onward band beside Ernest Trepagnier on bass drum, and explains drum and cymbal sizes, the beaters and two-four marching with four-four on the out chorus.

segments.chapter: Father and the brass band tradition
segments.title: Outstanding early parade drummers: Henry Martin, Red Dugal, Black Benny
segments.summary: He names the snare and bass drummers he followed as a boy and says they also played orchestra drums in district clubs.

segments.chapter: Father and the brass band tradition
segments.title: Brass band picnics and excursions
segments.summary: His father played picnics, excursions and fairground dances with the brass band, never in small groups; Barbarin was once sick at a picnic.

segments.chapter: Father and the brass band tradition
segments.title: Personnel of the Onward Brass Band
segments.summary: He lists the band members and their instruments, including Manuel Perez, Trepagnier, Eddie Cherrie, Adolph Alexander, the trombonists and tuba player; Bebe Matthews comes up as a drummer.

segments.title: Stick grip and roll technique
segments.summary: They discuss how drummers hold sticks, how fingers act as brakes, and that rolls are made from the wrist.

segments.title: Teaching and demonstrating rudiments on the pad
segments.summary: He mentions his teaching at Gateway and demonstrates five, seven and nine stroke rolls, open and closed rolls, rough, drag and press roll.

segments.title: His father's mellophone
segments.summary: They examine the silver mellophone his father gave him before he died, discuss how it was held, and his father's records.

segments.title: Kid Rena's band and Maurice French
segments.summary: He recalls clarinettist Maurice French in Kid Rena's band, now in Laplace, and sitting in for Joe Rena.

segments.title: Kid Rena band members and other clarinettists
segments.summary: He names men in Rena's band, including T-Boy and Zeb, and clarinettists George Abbott and Joe Watson who played by ear.

segments.title: Mutt Carey and the eggshell mute; replacing Zutty at the Elite
segments.summary: He worked with Mutt Carey, who used half an eggshell in his horn, and took over from Zutty Singleton.

segments.title: Zutty Singleton as a drummer
segments.summary: They praise Zutty as a fine drummer who played the Lyric Theater shows, and Russell returns to lessons.

segments.title: Collapsible folding drum set
segments.summary: He describes a drummer's collapsible duplex drum set that folded into one case.

segments.title: First piano player and house parties
segments.summary: His first piano player was Little Willie; they played house parties, which he recalls as better days with the district open.

segments.title: Imperial Serenaders: Albert Snaer, personnel and tailgate rivalry
segments.summary: He describes the Imperial Serenaders, Albert Snaer's wild trumpet, the full line-up, tailgate wagon contests with Kid Rena, and the Camellia band with George Stewart.

segments.title: Wooden Joe Nicholas as a trumpeter
segments.summary: He played with Wooden Joe in the Camellia band; Joe used ordinary mutes, played softly, but not mutes on parades.

segments.title: Buddy Petit, Kid Rena and Sharkey Bonano
segments.summary: He names Buddy Petit and Kid Rena as favourite high trumpeters and says Sharkey Bonano used to listen to Rena and plays close to him.

segments.title: The failed Columbia recording attempt
segments.summary: His only early attempt to record, for Columbia on Canal Street with Albert Snaer's band, produced a single side of 'Zozo'.

segments.title: Acoustic recording horns and his second set
segments.summary: He remembers recording into big horns before electric recording, and the set he bought after Paul's.

segments.title: His first set of drums from Paul
segments.summary: The first set was a single-tension light mahogany set from Grunewald with a 14 by 28 bass drum and Chinese cymbals.

segments.title: Later drum sets and sizes, modern drummers
segments.summary: He has owned about five sets, shrinking bass drums from 28 to 22, and discusses small drums and progressive drummers like Ed Blackwell.

segments.title: Rudiments, practice pad, sticks and wrist exercises
segments.summary: He still practises on a pad made by a student, and talks about stick weights, ebony sticks and parade versus dance sticks.

segments.title: Left-handed drummers and Baby Dodds
segments.summary: They discuss left-handed drummers Alfred Williams and Snags, and Barbarin says he never knew Baby Dodds or Minor Hall.

segments.title: Zutty's job at the Elite and the Tom Anderson club group
segments.summary: Zutty gave him his job at the Elite on Iberville; he played with Robichaux on the Madison steamer and in Paul's group at Tom Anderson's.
